---
title: "Ruby for non-Rubyists"
---

You do not need to become a Ruby programmer to read this book. Sonic Pi places a
music language on top of Ruby, and the examples use a deliberately small part of
the host language. This guide explains that part in the order you are likely to
notice it. If an example feels musically clear but syntactically unfamiliar,
start with the shape of its data, then use the relevant section here to decode
the punctuation.

## Symbols

`:c4` is a *symbol*, Ruby's compact way to represent a stable name. Sonic Pi
uses symbols for note names, synth names, and scale names, so the leading colon
appears in almost every lesson.

```ruby
play :c4          # symbol
play 60           # the same note as an integer
```

Symbols are ordinary values: they can sit in arrays and serve as hash keys.
Sonic Pi gives note symbols one additional musical ability. Inside its runtime,
`:c4 + 12` means the C one octave higher because the music layer converts the
note name before doing arithmetic. Plain Ruby does not treat arbitrary symbols
that way.

## Arrays and indexing

Most scores in the early chapters begin as arrays. Their indexes start at zero,
negative indexes count backward from the end, and a range selects a slice.

```ruby
notes = [60, 62, 64, 65]
notes[0]       # => 60
notes[-1]      # => 65
notes[1..2]    # => [62, 64]
```

`+` joins arrays and `rotate` moves values from the front to the back. The scale
and mode chapters use both. Methods with a trailing `!` usually mutate their
receiver; this book prefers the non-mutating form when score data is involved.

```ruby
[60, 64] + [67]          # => [60, 64, 67]
[0, 2, 4, 5].rotate(1)  # => [2, 4, 5, 0]
```

## Hashes and event data

A hash gives names to related values. That makes it a better representation
than parallel arrays once a note needs a start time, duration, and amplitude.
The event schema uses symbols as keys, and modern Ruby allows `note: 60` as
shorthand for `:note => 60`.

```ruby
event = {note: 60, start: 0, duration: 1, amp: 0.8}
event[:note]            # => 60
event.fetch(:duration)  # => 1
event.fetch(:pan, 0)    # => 0 when :pan is absent
```

`fetch` is useful when absence is an error or when a default should be visible.
Square-bracket lookup returns `nil` for a missing key, which can hide a spelling
mistake until the renderer runs.

## Blocks

A block is an anonymous function passed to a method. Ruby writes a longer block
with `do ... end` and often keeps a one-line block inside braces. Parameters go
between vertical bars. When you read the next example, translate it as "four
times, with the current count called `i`."

```ruby
4.times do |i|
  play 60 + i
  sleep 0.5
end
```

## each and map

The difference between `each` and `map` is one of the few Ruby distinctions that
shapes the musical model. `each` visits values for an effect such as playing a
note. `map` transforms the values and returns a new array, which is what a
transposition needs.

```ruby
[60, 64, 67].each { |n| play n; sleep 0.5 }
[60, 64, 67].map  { |n| n + 12 }              # => [72, 76, 79]
```

Destructuring works in block parameters, which is how the score walker reads
pairs:

```ruby
[[:c4, 1], [:e4, 0.5]].each do |pitch, duration|
  play pitch
  sleep duration
end
```

Several nearby methods appear in later lessons:

```ruby
[60, 62, 64].each_cons(2).to_a  # => [[60, 62], [62, 64]]
[60, 64, 67].zip([1, 1, 2])     # => [[60, 1], [64, 1], [67, 2]]
[1, 2, 3].sum                    # => 6
```

`each_cons(2)` exposes adjacent values, which suits interval and voice-leading
checks. `zip` aligns parallel arrays by index. `sum` is used for bar-duration
assertions.

## Conditions

Ruby's `if` is an expression, and a short condition can follow the statement it
controls.

```ruby
quality = interval == 4 ? :major : :minor
play note if note

if duration <= 0
  raise "duration must be positive"
end
```

Only `false` and `nil` are false in Ruby. Zero is true. That difference matters
when pitch class 0 represents C.

`case` works well for symbolic music data:

```ruby
offsets = case quality
          when :major then [0, 4, 7]
          when :minor then [0, 3, 7]
          else raise "unknown quality"
          end
```

## Keyword arguments

Trailing `name: value` pairs are keyword arguments. Sonic Pi uses them for the
features that shape a sound after the pitch is chosen.

```ruby
play :c4, amp: 0.7, release: 2, cutoff: 90
```

## Defining functions

Sonic Pi wraps Ruby's function definition in `define`. Registration with the
runtime makes the named function available inside threads and across repeated
runs. The examples still place every definition above its first call so that a
fresh buffer contains its whole explanation.

```ruby
define :play_phrase do |score, transpose: 0|
  score.each { |pitch, duration| play pitch + transpose; sleep duration }
end
```

Arguments before the keyword section are positional. A keyword with a default is
optional; one without a default is required. The final expression becomes the
return value.

```ruby
define :transpose do |notes, by:|
  notes.map { |n| n + by }
end

transpose([60, 64, 67], by: 12)
```

Keep definitions above their first call in a fresh buffer. Sonic Pi remembers a
named definition across runs, but examples in this book never depend on that
history.

## Rings

A ring is Sonic Pi's circular sequence type. Where an array eventually raises a
bounds error, a ring wraps around: `ring(1, 2, 3)[4]` returns `2`. This suits a
performance pattern that continues longer than the source sequence.

```ruby
notes = ring(:c4, :e4, :g4)
8.times { |i| play notes[i]; sleep 0.5 }   # cycles, no bounds error
```

Sonic Pi adds `tick` and `look` for counters associated with the current thread.
`tick` advances and returns the counter; `look` reads it without advancing.

```ruby
notes = ring(:c4, :e4, :g4)
6.times do
  play notes.tick
  sleep 0.5
end
```

An explicit loop index is easier to inspect when several rings must advance at
different rates. The book uses `tick` for repeating performance patterns and an
index for transformations whose positions carry meaning.

## Numeric details

Pitch arithmetic uses integers, but beat arithmetic often needs a floating-point
value. In Ruby 2.6, `2 / 3` uses integer division and loses the triplet; `2.0 /
3` preserves it. Modulo performs a different kind of reduction, wrapping an
unbounded note address into a pitch class or an event count into a pattern slot.

```ruby
61 % 12       # => 1, the pitch class C-sharp or D-flat
2.0 / 3       # => 0.6666666666666666
13 % 4        # => 1, the second slot in a four-step pattern
```

Floating-point duration sums can carry tiny rounding errors. A check over many
fractional events should compare within a tolerance instead of demanding exact
equality.

## Threads and shared state

`in_thread` and `live_loop` let musical lines advance concurrently under Sonic
Pi's deterministic scheduler. Local variables are captured when a thread
begins. Long-lived loops coordinate more clearly through `cue` and `sync`, while
`set` and `get` provide named state when a value genuinely needs to change.

Prefer messages and immutable score data to shared mutable arrays. A live loop
that reads a changing array while another loop writes it is harder to reason
about than two loops starting from the same cue and reading stable data.

## Things that trip you up

Several small rules account for a large share of confusing failures. Ruby
returns the last expression, so functions rarely need `return`. Integer
division truncates, which makes `2.0 / 3` the safe spelling for a triplet.
Symbols and strings are different types, and Sonic Pi usually expects symbols
for musical names. A method name may end in `?`; the punctuation does not change
the call syntax, but it tells the reader to expect a Boolean result.
